question: The rapid expansion of data centres and AI infrastructure threatens to cause electricity consumption in the European Union to skyrocket, resulting in network congestion and putting a strain on Europe’s decarbonisation objectives.

Recently, the media has reported1 that technology companies have been pressuring European organisations in the renewable sector regarding a proposal by Greenhouse Gas Protocol to tighten disclosure rules on power emissions and introduce geographical and temporal correlation criteria for tech giants’ renewable energy certificates.
This highlights the growing contradiction between tech giants’ climate commitments and the energy impact of their AI and their data centres. 1.
Is the Commission aware that the industry is exerting pressure in this regard?

How will it ensure that there are independent and auditable verification mechanisms to monitor companies’ self-declarations about their data centres’ sustainability indicators, so as to prevent greenwashing and false statements?
Will it introduce, under its 2026 work programme, additional transparency obligations2 regarding data centres’ energy consumption and carbon footprint?

Directive (EU) 2023/1791 and Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1364.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (7.4.2026) The 2050 climate-neutrality objective entails the need to ensure that digital growth is powered by clean, resilient, and sustainable energy. To this end, the Commission engages with all involved parties and stakeholders and follows closely relevant discussions.

The Commission announced a Data Centre Energy Efficiency Package1, which will be published together with the Strategy Roadmap on Digitalisation and AI in 2026. The Data Centre Energy Efficiency Package will build on the current reporting scheme for data centres2 and aims at introducing an EU wide rating scheme and label for the energy efficiency and sustainability of data centres.

It will also launch an open public consultation for the establishment of minimum performance standards for data centres in Europe and assess how transparency could be increased and most sustainable practices in the industry could be promoted.

To prepare the ground for these initiatives, the Commission has evaluated, among others, the quality of the data reported by data centre operators3 and is working with Member States to take further measures to ensure accurate reporting.

A report to the European Parliament and the Council providing an assessment of the European data centres sector, based on the first reporting period, and proposed actions to be taken will be published soon.
